items.title: Working the anomaly score by hand
items.body:
`scoreLogAnomaly` adds `logLevelWeight(level) * environmentWeight(environment)` per log: warn is 8 and staging is 0.8, so each log adds 6.4 and three add 19.2. A fingerprint that appears 3 or more times adds `count * 10`, here 30. There is no fatal log, fewer than 5 errors, and no timeout or auth words, so the total is 49.2, rounded to 49. `shouldCreateIncident` requires `score >= 70` AND at least one production log; both fail.

- 79 would need another 30 points, and the incident flag needs production anyway.
- 19 forgets the repeated-fingerprint bonus.
- 100 is the clamp ceiling, far above this total.

items.title: In an else-if chain, the first match wins
items.body:
The joined lowercase messages contain "token", "timeout" and "db". Three branches could match, but they form one `if / else if / else if` chain. The auth regex is tested first and matches "token", so the agent sets "Authentication degradation" and skips the rest.

- "Database or performance degradation" would win only if no auth word were present.
- "Third-party integration failure" needs webhook, integration, third-party, rate limit or 429.
- "Operational noise" is the default when no branch matches.

Compare this with the job agent, where separate `if` blocks let the LAST match win.

items.title: The registry checks the target before running
items.body:
`runRegisteredAgent` looks up the agent, then checks `agent.supportedTargets.includes(request.targetType)`. The log anomaly agent declares `supportedTargets: ["LOG_GROUP", "INCIDENT"]`, so a JOB target fails the check and the function throws `${agentType} does not support target ${request.targetType}` without calling `agent.run`.

- "Runs on an empty log list" would need the check to pass; it does not.
- "A FAILED result object" is wrong: the registry throws, it does not build a result. (In the worker, that throw marks the AgentRun FAILED.)
- "Falls back to another agent" is wrong: the registry looks up exactly one agent by type and never searches.

excerpts.quote: throw new Error(`${agentType} does not support target ${request.targetType}`);

items.title: A helper that nothing calls protects nothing
items.body:
`updateTicketAction` starts with `requireActionUser("ticket.update", "ticket:update")`, and MANAGER holds `ticket:update`. It then loads the ticket in the user's organization and calls `assertTicketTransition`. IN_PROGRESS may move to RESOLVED, so the update succeeds. `canResolveTickets`, which leaves MANAGER out, exists in `tickets.ts` but no action or page calls it.

- "canResolveTickets throws" assumes the helper is wired in; it is not.
- "IN_PROGRESS cannot reach RESOLVED" is wrong: RESOLVED is in its allowed list.
- "Set to ESCALATED instead" is not something the action ever does; it stores the submitted status.

Lesson: a rule only exists where the server enforces it.

items.title: Fingerprints ignore the numbers in a message
items.body:
`createLogFingerprint` normalizes the message before hashing: lowercase, replace runs of 8 or more hex characters with an id placeholder, then replace any run of digits with an n placeholder, collapse spaces. Both messages become the same normalized text: order, the n placeholder, failed. With the same service and level, the SHA-1 input `service:level:message` is identical, so the fingerprints match. That is the purpose: group the same error across different ids.

- "Hashed exactly as written" skips the normalization steps.
- "Only 8+ hex ids are normalized" misses the second replace, which handles any digits.
- The request id is not part of the hash input at all.

items.title: A new priority recomputes the SLA from creation time
items.body:
In `updateTicketAction`, when the priority changes the action stores `calculateSlaDueAt(nextPriority, before.createdAt)`. CRITICAL is 2 hours in `slaHoursByPriority`, and the base is the creation time, 09:00, so the new deadline is 11:00. At 15:00 that is already four hours in the past, and the ticket shows as breached.

- "Two hours from the change" would need `new Date()` as the base; the code passes `before.createdAt`.
- "The old 72-hour deadline" is kept only when the priority did NOT change.
- 36 hours is the MEDIUM window and has nothing to do with this change.

excerpts.quote: slaDueAt: nextPriority !== before.priority ? calculateSlaDueAt(nextPriority, before.createdAt) : before.slaDueAt
const slaHoursByPriority: Record<TicketPriority, number> = { LOW: 72, MEDIUM: 36, HIGH: 8, CRITICAL: 2

items.title: Start here: a help desk with rule-based agents and a worker
items.body:
AgentDesk is an internal help desk: tickets, incidents, structured logs, background jobs and audit events. On top sit three "agents" that look like AI analysis but are plain deterministic rules: ticket summarization, log anomaly detection and failed job investigation. No model is called.

Read in this order. `docs/05-domain-model-guide.md` names the entities and the SLA rules. `docs/03-agent-system-guide.md` explains the agent interface and the registry. `docs/04-observability-and-debugging-guide.md` covers fingerprints and anomaly scoring. Then `docs/10-production-hardening-implementation.md` and `docs/12-audit-change-study-guide.md` describe the later hardening pass: organization scoping, queued agent runs and a database-backed worker.

The guides summarize; the answers live in the code. Keep `packages/domain/src`, `packages/agents/src`, `apps/web/lib/actions.ts` and `packages/db/src/worker.ts` open, and read rule blocks in order, because order often decides the result.

excerpts.quote: The agent system is local, deterministic, and fully mocked.

readMore.why: A suggested file-by-file reading order for the whole codebase.
The change map table: each audit gap, its new invariant and where it lives.

items.title: A conditional update is the claim
items.body:
Both workers can read the same candidate with `findFirst`, since that read takes no lock. The real claim is `updateMany` with `where: { id, status: { in: ["QUEUED", "RETRYING"] } }`. The first update changes the status to RUNNING. The second finds no row that still has a claimable status, so `claimed.count` is 0 and `claimNextJob` returns null; the caller treats that as idle.

- "Both run it" ignores the status predicate on the update.
- "updateMany throws on a locked row" is wrong: a non-matching `updateMany` simply reports count 0.
- "Both mark it RUNNING" would need the second update to match, which it cannot.

Compare this with an update `where` that names only the id: that version has no claim.

excerpts.quote: const claimed = await prisma.backgroundJob.updateMany({ where: { id: candidate.id, status: { in: ["QUEUED", "RETRYING"] } },

items.title: Concept: heuristic agents are ordered rule lists
items.body:
Each agent is a `run(request)` function that starts from default values and then walks a list of regular-expression checks over the input text. Two shapes appear, and they behave differently.

In the failed job agent, every check is its own `if`. Several can match the same error message, and each one that matches assigns the shared variables again, so a later block can replace what an earlier block decided. In the log anomaly agent, the signature checks are an `if / else if` chain, so only the FIRST matching branch runs.

When you predict an agent's output, list which regexes match, then apply them in source order with that difference in mind. Also check the steps after the rules: attempt counts and linked incidents adjust risk and escalation at the end. The registry adds one more gate before any of this runs: the target type must be one the agent supports.

readMore.why: runRegisteredAgent: the target-type check that runs before any agent.

items.title: The last matching rule writes the recommendation
items.body:
The message matches two blocks. "Invalid payload", "malformed" and "json" match the payload block at line 55, which sets "Do not retry until the payload or producer code is corrected." But "429" and "rate limit" match the rate-limit block at line 76, which runs later and assigns `retryRecommendation` again: "Retry with exponential backoff and jitter." Attempts are 1 of 3, so the max-attempts block does not replace it.

- The payload advice is what a careful reader wants, but it is overwritten.
- "Retry with backoff; this class is usually safe to retry." needs timeout or network words, and there are none.
- "Retry once after reviewing recent worker logs." is only the default before any rule matches.

This is a real weakness: `nonRetryableUntilFixed` stays true while the advice says retry.

excerpts.quote: retryRecommendation = "Retry with exponential backoff and jitter.";

items.title: A linked SEV1 incident raises the risk to critical
items.body:
"timed out" matches the timeout block, which changes the cause and advice but leaves `riskLevel` at its default, "medium". Attempts are below the maximum, so that block is skipped. Then the incident block runs: any related incident sets `escalationNeeded = true`, and the risk becomes "critical" when the severity is SEV1, otherwise "high".

- "medium" would be right without the incident link; the link changes it.
- "high for every linked incident" misses the SEV1 special case on line 95.
- "low" is never assigned anywhere in this agent.

items.title: CLOSED is the only terminal ticket status
items.body:
`canTransitionTicket` first returns true when `from === to`, then looks the target up in `allowedTicketTransitions[from]`. CLOSED maps to `[]`, so CLOSED to IN_PROGRESS fails and `assertTicketTransition` throws.

- RESOLVED to IN_PROGRESS is allowed: RESOLVED lists CLOSED and IN_PROGRESS, so a resolved ticket can be reopened.
- CLOSED to CLOSED is allowed by the same-status shortcut, which lets an edit that keeps the status pass.
- NEW to CLOSED is allowed: NEW lists CLOSED directly.

items.title: Concept: agent runs and jobs go through a database worker
items.body:
After the hardening pass, clicking "Run Agent" no longer runs the agent inside the request. The server action writes an `AgentRun` row and an `AGENT_RUN` background job, and a separate worker process picks the job up later.

Three things to watch in `packages/db/src/worker.ts`. First, how a worker claims a job: it finds a candidate, then updates it with a `where` that repeats the expected status, and checks how many rows changed. Second, what the worker does with `attempts` and `maxAttempts` when a job throws, and who increments `attempts` (the claim, or someone else?). Third, how the agent run row moves through its statuses and where an error message is stored.

The guide calls this "a database-backed worker, not a full queue system". Keep that limit in mind.

excerpts.quote: The worker claims queued or retrying jobs, marks them running, executes handlers, updates status, and writes audit events.

readMore.why: The full worker: claim, process, and the success and failure paths.

items.title: Nobody increments attempts on a worker run
items.body:
`queueAgentRun` creates the `AGENT_RUN` job with `attempts: 0` and `maxAttempts: 1`. `claimNextJob` sets status, lock and start time, but does not change `attempts`. When processing throws, the worker computes `job.attempts >= job.maxAttempts ? "DEAD_LETTERED" : "FAILED"`; 0 >= 1 is false, so the job is FAILED.

- DEAD_LETTERED would need attempts to reach 1 first, which only `retryJobAction` does.
- RETRYING is set by the retry action, not by the worker.
- "The claim raised attempts" is wrong: the claim data has no `attempts` field.

So `canRetryJob(FAILED, 0, 1)` is true and an operator can retry it once.

items.title: A late resolution still counts as a breach
items.body:
`getSlaState` handles finished tickets first. For RESOLVED or CLOSED it returns "breached" when `resolvedAt` exists and is later than `slaDueAt`, otherwise "resolved". This ticket was resolved one hour late, so the answer is "breached".

- "resolved" is only for tickets finished on time.
- "approaching" and the 4-hour window apply only to open tickets; the early return means a finished ticket never reaches that code.
- "The clock stops at resolution" is half right: it stops, but the stop time is compared with the deadline.
